title: The messianic age
hookLine: Maimonides pictures the world running as usual, but without war or hunger

cards: Sunrise. A baker unlocks the shop. Buses run.
Children argue about whose turn it is. Nothing about the morning looks miraculous. And yet nobody anywhere is marching to war, and nobody anywhere goes to bed hungry.
That ordinary-looking morning is close to how Maimonides describes the days of the messiah, in the closing chapters of his law code. Not fire from the sky. Not a new set of physics.
The same world, with the worst things gone.

teach.b: The messianic age. Maimonides closes the Mishneh Torah with it, in the Laws of Kings. First, the world keeps its habits.
Don't imagine, he writes, that anything of the world's ordinary order will be canceled, or that something new will enter creation.
He quotes a sage in the Talmud: the only difference between this world and the days of the messiah is that Israel will no longer be subject to the rule of other kingdoms.

teach.h: THE WOLF AND THE LAMB, A PARABLE.
teach.b: Second, the wolf and the lamb. Isaiah says, "And the wolf shall dwell with the lamb." Maimonides reads it as a parable: nations once fierce as wolves will live in peace.
How it will all happen, nobody will know until it does. The prophets' words are unclear, and sages disagreed. So he warns readers not to get lost calculating the details.
The sages didn't long for those days to rule the world, or to eat and drink and celebrate, he writes, but to be free to study and to know God, with nothing pressing on them.
There will be no famine and no war, no envy and no rivalry. Good things will be plentiful, and the whole world's occupation will be to know God.

teach.h: AS THE WATERS COVER THE SEA.
teach.b: He ends the entire code with Isaiah: "for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea."
Jews hold a range of views on the messiah today, and some streams speak more of a messianic age than a person. This is his picture: ordinary days, made safe.

how: The traditional daily prayers ask for redemption, and the Aleinu prayer, said near the end of services, looks toward a world united in knowing God. Some communities connect that hope to feeding the hungry and working for peace now.

o: an ordinary world without war or hunger, free to know God
the yearly fast that marks the Temple's fall
a golden age that already ended with King Solomon

games.q: the messianic age — tap the pairs.
p: goes on in its usual way
a parable of peace among nations
as the waters cover the sea

s: Maimonides says the laws of nature will change in the messianic age
he says the world goes on in its usual way; nothing of its order is canceled.
he reads the wolf and the lamb as a parable
the fierce nations, like wolves, will live in peace.
he says the sages longed for those days so they could rule the world
he says they longed to be free to study and know God.

games.q: you're reading Isaiah: the wolf shall dwell with the lamb. a friend asks if Maimonides expects wolves to stop hunting. what does he say?
o: it's a parable: nations will live in peace.
games.why: he reads it as a parable. the world keeps its natural order; what changes is that war and hunger are gone.

practice: Picture tomorrow morning where you live, your street, your kitchen, the people nearby, and take one thing out of the picture: somebody in your town who is hungry.
See the morning without that, and ask plainly what one step this week moves toward it, a bag of groceries, a meal for a neighbor, a small recurring gift.
If you pray, you can hold the words "as the waters cover the sea" for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: The messianic age. In Maimonides' telling, the world running as it always has, but without war, hunger, envy or rivalry, so that people are free to know God. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the days of the messiah, the phrase Maimonides uses for the age he describes.

carryVoice: Your line: the world, at peace. The same world, with the worst things gone. Rest well.
